nameStory: The Brick Cap gets its name from its striking resemblance to a weathered red brick! When you spot these mushrooms clustered on rotting logs, their rusty reddish-brown caps look just like miniature bricks scattered through the forest. The color is so distinctive that once you see it, you'll never forget why early mushroom hunters chose this practical name.
description: Brick Caps are medium-sized mushrooms that grow in dense clusters on decaying hardwood logs and stumps. They have distinctive brick-red to reddish-brown caps that can reach 2-4 inches across, with yellowish gills underneath that darken with age. The stems are typically pale yellow to brownish and often have a slight ring zone. These saprophytic fungi are wood decomposers, helping break down dead trees in New England's forests.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Brick-red to reddish-brown color, smooth and slightly sticky when moist, becoming dry and sometimes cracking with age

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Start pale yellow or whitish, gradually turning olive-brown to purplish-brown as spores mature, attached to the stem

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Pale yellow to brownish, often with a faint ring zone near the top, hollow or stuffed with white pith

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Dark purplish-brown to nearly black when collected on white paper

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Mild to slightly bitter or unpleasant odor, not particularly distinctive

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Always grows in dense clusters or clumps on hardwood logs, stumps, and buried wood - never solitary. SAFETY NOTE: Never eat wild mushrooms without expert identification, as this genus contains poisonous look-alikes.

habitat: Brick Caps thrive on decaying hardwood logs, stumps, and buried wood throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. You'll find them especially common on oak, maple, and beech wood in moist woodland areas. They prefer the partially shaded environment of forest floors and woodland edges where fallen logs provide their preferred substrate.

seasonality.spring: Rarely fruiting in late spring, but mycelium is actively growing within decaying wood as temperatures warm and moisture increases.
seasonality.summer: Occasional fruiting during wet periods, but hot, dry conditions typically inhibit mushroom production.
seasonality.fall: Peak fruiting season from September through November, especially after autumn rains when temperatures cool and humidity rises.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting bodies disappear with hard frosts, though the mycelium continues growing slowly within the wood substrate.

funFact: Brick Caps can actually glow very faintly in the dark! Their mycelium (the fungal threads inside rotting wood) produces a subtle bioluminescence called foxfire, creating an eerie green glow that was once used by loggers to mark trails through dark forests.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the poisonous Sulphur Tuft, which grows in similar clusters on wood. Remember: Brick Caps have brick-red caps while Sulphur Tufts are bright yellow-green. When in doubt, check the cap color first - if it's not clearly brick-red, it's likely a different species entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Brick Caps are also called 'chestnut mushrooms' in some field guides, but this name is confusing because it's also used for completely different edible mushrooms sold in grocery stores. Stick with 'Brick Cap' to avoid mix-ups, and remember that the brick-red color is your best identification clue.
compareHints: Among its Hypholoma relatives, Brick Cap stands out with its distinctive brick-red coloring - Sulphur Tuft is bright yellow-green and poisonous, while Smoky-gilled Hypholoma has grayish caps and whitish gills that don't turn olive-brown. The Brick Cap's reddish-brown cap color is unique in this genus and makes it the easiest to identify safely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its close relative the brick cap which has reddish-brown colors and milder taste, sulphur tuft stays bright yellow and is intensely bitter.
